readingInstruction: Read 3 John, a single chapter. It is a private letter to a friend named Gaius, with a contrast between two men in the church: Gaius, who welcomed missionaries, and Diotrephes, who refused them. Notice how generosity and pride show themselves in practice.
settingTheScene: Third John is the companion to 2 John. In 2 John, John warns against receiving false teachers. In 3 John, he commends receiving true ones. Traveling missionaries went out “for the sake of the name,” relying on the hospitality of local believers rather than taking support from pagans. Gaius had welcomed them, and a leader named Diotrephes had not. The letter gives a window into the ordinary life of a first-century church with its generosity, ambition, and conflict.
observation: “Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul” (v. 2).
“I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (v. 4).
“Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are” (v. 5).
“For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (v. 7).
“Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (v. 8).
“Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first” (v. 9).
“Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good” (v. 11).
“Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone” (v. 12).
interpretation:
John writes to “the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.” His first words are a prayer for health: “I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.” It is a common greeting that implies that Gaius’s soul was doing well. It is not a promise that all believers will be healthy and wealthy but a loving wish for a friend. John rejoices when brothers testify to Gaius’s truth. “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” For a spiritual father, there is no greater joy.

Gaius is praised for his hospitality: “it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are.” They have testified to his love before the church. John urges him to send them on their journey “in a manner worthy of God.” Why? “For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.” When we support missionaries, teachers, and church planters, we share in their work. This is a strong argument for generosity in giving and hospitality.

By contrast, Diotrephes “likes to put himself first.” He does not acknowledge John’s authority. He is “talking wicked nonsense against us,” will not welcome the brothers, and even stops those who want to, putting them out of the church. We should not be surprised that even the early church had its power struggles. Pride is the opposite of the servant spirit of Christ. John plans to deal with him personally when he comes.

John then gives a principle: “Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.” Our conduct reveals our relationship with God. Demetrius, probably the one who carried the letter, is commended as a model. He has a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself.

The letter closes with the hope of seeing Gaius face to face: “Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.” Christian friendship is personal, valuing each by name. This tiny letter reminds us that the work of the gospel depends on ordinary acts of generosity as well as on great teachers.
connection: Romans 12:13, 1 Peter 4:9, and Hebrews 13:2 command hospitality. Matthew 10:9-14 describes how Jesus sent out his disciples to rely on hospitality. Philippians 4:14-18 commends partnership in giving. Titus 3:13 also speaks of sending teachers on their way. Mark 9:33-35 and 10:42-45 teach that greatness is service. 1 Peter 5:3 warns elders against domineering. Matthew 23:5-12 warns against love of honor. Luke 22:24-27 shows the disciples’ own ambition. Philippians 2:3-4 calls us to humility.
application:
Is there a missionary, church planter, or a visiting speaker you could support with prayer, money, or hospitality? Do it this week.

Ask whether you ever “like to put yourself first” in your family, church, or workplace. Confess it and take a lower seat.

Write a note to someone who has been a Gaius to you, and thank them by name.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for friends who walk in the truth.
Ask him to make you generous to those who serve him.
Ask him to keep you from loving to be first.
